clinicalPearls: A benign chronic inflammatory dermatosis of the glans and prepuce, occurring almost exclusively in uncircumcised men
It presents as a well-demarcated, shiny, red-orange plaque, sometimes with pinpoint (cayenne pepper) spots
It is a diagnosis often confirmed by biopsy showing a dense plasma-cell infiltrate
Chronic irritation under the foreskin, with poor aeration and retained smegma, is thought to drive it
The main concern is to exclude erythroplasia of Queyrat (penile carcinoma in situ) and lichen planus
It often responds to improved hygiene, topical anti-inflammatory treatment, and definitively to circumcision
reference.pathophysiology: Zoon balanitis is a chronic reactive mucosal inflammation of the glans and prepuce characterised histologically by a band-like dermal infiltrate rich in plasma cells. It is thought to result from chronic low-grade irritation, friction, moisture and retained smegma beneath the foreskin, since it occurs in uncircumcised men and typically resolves after circumcision. It is not an infection or a premalignant condition, though its appearance overlaps with penile carcinoma in situ, necessitating exclusion of the latter.
additionalDifferentials: Erythroplasia of Queyrat (penile carcinoma in situ)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of the characteristic plaque
Biopsy to confirm plasma-cell infiltrate and exclude carcinoma in situ
Swabs to exclude infective balanitis where relevant
Assessment of foreskin and hygiene factors
Follow-up to ensure resolution and exclude malignancy
redFlags: Features suggesting erythroplasia of Queyrat or invasive carcinoma
Failure to respond to conservative treatment
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often resolves with conservative measures or circumcision, though it can be chronic and relapsing if predisposing factors persist.
pitfalls: Missing penile carcinoma in situ, which can look similar
Treating it as candidal balanitis without response
Not biopsying a persistent or atypical lesion
Overlooking the role of the foreskin and hygiene
management: Circumcision offers definitive cure by removing the retained smegma, moisture and friction that drive the inflammation, and is the treatment of choice for persistent or relapsing disease
Optimise local hygiene as first-line conservative care, with regular gentle retraction and cleansing, drying of the glans and preputial sac, and reduction of friction and smegma retention
Topical anti-inflammatory therapy with corticosteroids, sometimes combined with an antimicrobial, or topical calcineurin inhibitors as a steroid-sparing option for symptomatic plaques

Confirm the diagnosis by biopsy showing the band-like plasma-cell infiltrate and actively exclude erythroplasia of Queyrat (penile carcinoma in situ) and lichen planus before committing to long-term conservative treatment
Identify and treat any co-existing infective balanitis, whether candidal or bacterial, contributing to preputial inflammation

Refer to dermatology or urology for diagnostic uncertainty, atypical or non-resolving lesions and for circumcision, keeping lesions under review with re-biopsy of any that fail to resolve to exclude malignancy
